Reproductive investment in the whitecheek surgeonfish, Acanthurus nigricans, shows a pattern common among acanthurids sampled near Pacific coral reef habitats. Field surveys of this species at a mean water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] yielded a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 9% [GSI = 9%]. This index was derived from gravimetric analysis of ovarian and somatic tissue in reproductively active females. The measurement aligns with values reported for the congener Acanthurus nigrofuscus and points toward an iteroparous life-history strategy where somatic growth is prioritized alongside annual breeding effort. Such a low index implies that the species relies more on frequent, low-volume spawning events rather than a single massive gamete release, a tactic that may buffer against variable recruitment success in dynamic reef environments.

From larval rearing studies and otolith back-calculation, the ultimate total length that Acanthurus nigricans attains in undisturbed populations is 36 cm [Li = 36 cm], placing it among the medium-sized surgeonfishes within its genus. This asymptotic size is achieved after several years of sustained growth on coral-rich foraging grounds. The wet weight that corresponds to that maximum recorded body length, calculated from standard length-weight regressions, is 955 grams [Wwi = 955 grams], a substantial body mass that supports the species’ role as a mobile grazer on epilithic algal turfs. In contrast, the initial mass at the onset of life is remarkably small. Based on the average diameter of a fertilized ovum, which measures approximately 0.7 mm, the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a fact that underscores the extreme vulnerability of the pelagic larval stage. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are therefore minute, lecithotrophic organisms that must rely entirely on endogenous reserves before transitioning to planktivory.

The onset of reproductive capability is marked by a distinct size threshold at puberty. Field collections and gonad inspection indicate that Acanthurus nigricans reaches sexual maturity at a total length of 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm], a measurement that corresponds to roughly half the species’ ultimate length. The wet weight at which puberty typically occurs, derived from the same length-weight relationship used for adults, is 125 grams [Wwp = 125 grams]. This size at first maturity is consistent with a life-history model in which individuals allocate resources toward somatic growth during early life and only initiate gametogenesis once a critical body size has been achieved. The shift from juvenile to reproductively viable organism is thus a gradual process, and the 125 gram threshold suggests that a significant period of feeding and energy storage on the reef is necessary before an individual can successfully participate in seasonal spawning aggregations. This strategy likely enhances fecundity at first reproduction.

Longevity records for Acanthurus nigricans, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by annual increment counts on sagittal otoliths, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 34 years [am = approximately 34 years] when the fish are resident at their typical ambient temperature at a temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. This exceptional lifespan, nearly three and a half decades, was documented in a population inhabiting waters that average 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], a thermal regime that appears to support slow but steady somatic growth without accelerating senescence. Such a long life places the whitecheek surgeonfish among the more durable members of the Acanthuridae, rivaling some larger-bodied reef herbivores. The extended lifespan likely confers a demographic advantage by allowing multiple reproductive seasons across a prolonged adult phase, thereby buffering the population against occasional recruitment failures. It stands in stark contrast to the brief, high-mortality existence of its pelagic larvae, highlighting a dramatic ontogenetic shift in survival prospects.

Comparing life-history traits across the chronologically ordered stages reveals a fascinating contrast in growth efficiency. The journey from a minuscule 0.00018 gram [Wwb = 0.00018 gram] hatchling to a mature adult of 125 grams [Wwp = 125 grams] represents a mass increase spanning nearly six orders of magnitude, a feat achieved through efficient algal grazing during the juvenile and sub-adult phases. Furthermore, the continuous somatic growth from 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm] at puberty to the 36 cm [Li = 36 cm] ultimate total length demonstrates a capacity for post-maturational expansion that is relatively uncommon among reef fishes. The long-term persistence of individuals up to approximately 34 years [am = up to approximately 34 years] at 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] allows this growth to unfold gradually, minimizing the metabolic demands of rapid expansion in favor of a sustained, steady increase in body size. This suite of parameters paints a demographic portrait of a slow-paced, resilient species well-adapted to the predictable yet competitive environment of the Indo-Pacific reef flat.
